keySentence: Milo was bored with everything — until a magic tollbooth changed his whole world.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: Milo thought that nothing in the world was interesting or worth paying attention to at all. He could not understand why anyone got excited about school or hobbies or any other thing. But then a strange purple tollbooth appeared in his room one afternoon without any warning. He drove through it in his toy car and arrived in a kingdom he had never imagined before. In this new world every word and every number was alive and important and full of meaning. Milo realized with surprise that the world had always been this interesting — he just had not looked. Milo was bored with everything — until a magic tollbooth changed his whole world.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: The Milo who arrived home after school that particular afternoon was the same Milo as always. He dropped his bag, sat at his desk, and prepared for another evening of comfortable nothing. Then he saw the package and the tollbooth and the map and something shifted very slightly inside him. He had nothing to lose by driving through a small booth in his own bedroom so he went ahead and did it. What he found on the other side was a world organized entirely around things he had always dismissed as dull. Words were taken with absolute seriousness and numbers were treated as more precious than any physical treasure. The Milo who drove back through the tollbooth weeks later was not the same Milo who had been bored with everything. Milo was bored with everything — until a magic tollbooth changed his whole world.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: The transformation that Milo undergoes in The Phantom Tollbooth is not the result of magic in any simple sense. He does not return from his journey with new abilities or knowledge that he lacked before he left his bedroom. What he returns with is something more fundamental and more durable — the habit of paying genuine attention. Juster's genius is to construct a world in which the things Milo finds most boring at home are revealed as endlessly rich. Words, which he barely notices, turn out to contain entire kingdoms of meaning, humor, ambiguity, and consequence. Numbers, which he ignores, turn out to underpin everything beautiful and orderly in the landscape around him. The tollbooth did not deliver Milo to a better world — it delivered him to a better version of his own perception. And that is the transformation that lasts, because it requires no tollbooth to maintain once it has genuinely begun. Milo was bored with everything — until a magic tollbooth changed his whole world.
